scenario: AITA for not helping a woman at walmart | I (male 24) started working at walmart for the summer about a month ago. My job mainly involves working with inventory in the back room and not on the floor with customers, sometimes we get heavy boxes that we need to lift as a part of our regular duties. One of my co-workers is a female (fcw) in her early to mid 30s, physically in good shape and as far as I can tell no physical disabilities. (Fcw) approaches me and asks if I can help her lift a heavy box, I say of course and I walk over to the box with her expecting us to perform a team lift - however we get to the box and as I get to one side of the box expecting her to go to the other she just stands there and watches me. I ask "are you ready?" And she says "yes it just needs to go in that bin" (referencing a metal shelving unit about 4 feet high). I say "ok let's do it" and she responds "it's to heavy for me can you please lift it into the bin?". I respond by saying "I'm more than happy to help anyone if they're having trouble with something, but I'm not going to lift all your heavy boxes for you while you stand there watching me" and (fcw) said "if you're not willing to help me I'll find someone who will" and stormed off. Later on the head guy on our team (not my boss just the guy with most seniority who directs us) walks up to me and said " I just spoke to (fcw), the next time someone asks for help you need to help them, that's part of being a team. I responded by clarifying exactly what happened in case she stretched the truth and finished by saying "we're both paid to do the exact same job and if she cant perform the tasks then she shouldn't have taken the job, I'm not the designated heavy lifter on our team and if you would like to discuss this further we can do it with HR present", and at this point feeling pretty annoyed, it was my turn to storm off. So, was I the asshole in this situation? Because so far it seems like its 2 against 1.

First, the situation: A male employee at Walmart, let's call him John, has been working there for a month. His job involves handling inventory in the back room, which includes lifting heavy boxes. One of his coworkers is a woman in her early to mid-30s, physically fit with no apparent disabilities. She approaches John and asks for help lifting a heavy box. John agrees, expecting a team lift. But when they get to the box, she just stands there and watches him. John asks if she's ready, and she says yes, pointing to a bin about 4 feet high. She then asks him to lift the box into the bin because it's too heavy for her. John responds that he's happy to help if she's struggling but isn't going to lift all her boxes while she stands by. She gets upset and storms off. Later, the team leader talks to John, telling him that helping is part of the team and that he should have done it. John defends himself, saying they're both paid to do the same job and if she can't handle it, she shouldn't have taken the job. He also mentions HR. Now, the question is: Was John the asshole? Hmm. Let's consider the perspectives. On one hand, John is a new employee, and he's being asked to do a task that's part of his job. He agreed to help but expected a team effort. When the coworker didn't lift her part, he felt it was unfair to do all the work. He also pointed out that they're both paid to do the same job, implying that she should be able to handle her tasks. On the other hand, the coworker felt she needed help and was upset when he refused. The team leader backed her up, saying it's part of being a team. I think it's important to consider workplace dynamics. In a team, helping each other out is generally encouraged, especially when someone is struggling. However, there's a line between being helpful and being taken advantage of. If the coworker is physically fit and capable, it might be reasonable for John to expect her to contribute. But if she genuinely needed help, maybe John should have been more accommodating, especially since he's the new guy and might want to build good relationships with his coworkers. Another angle is the team leader's perspective. He told John that helping is part of the team, which suggests that the company culture values teamwork and support. By refusing, John might have come across as uncooperative, which could affect his standing in the team. However, John also had a point about both being paid to do the same job. If the coworker can't handle her tasks, that's a different issue, but in this case, she asked for help, so it's about whether to assist or not. I'm leaning towards John not being entirely in the wrong, but maybe he could have handled it differently. Perhaps he could have asked her to help lift, making it a team effort, instead of refusing outright. That way, he still helps but doesn't do all the work alone. Alternatively, he could have explained his willingness to help in a team effort but not to do all the lifting for her. In the end, it's a bit of a gray area. John's refusal might have been seen as uncooperative, but his expectation of teamwork is also valid. The team leader's intervention adds pressure, making it seem like John was the asshole, but there's more nuance to it.
